Rest of today through Sunday night: The surface is dry with dew 
point temperatures ranging from the teens to single digits in 
the Methow, Sinlahekin, and Okanogan Valley to the mid 20s and 
mid 30s across the rest of eastern WA into the ID Panhandle. 
There is a tightly wound low pressure system spinning off of the
northern coast of Vancouver Island. The western portion of WA 
state and north-central WA are located within the warm sector 
of this low pressure system. Moisture aloft has been increasing 
resulting in thickening cloud cover. Precipitation is being 
observed across northwest WA, but it's too dry over north- 
central WA for anything but virga falling out of the base of the
clouds. The prognoses over the next 24-36 hours is for the low 
to drop south off of the coast of WA. Moisture will stay closer 
in proximity to the center of the low resulting in continue dry 
forecast for most of the Inland Northwest. We do introduce a 
20-40% probability of precipitation along the east slopes of the
Cascades by late Sunday afternoon and evening.

Monday through Tuesday: Model ensembles are consolidating around the 
scenario of the upper level low pressure system to track near the 
OR/WA border Monday into Monday night. There are fringe solutions 
such as the NAM that tracks the low further north over north-central 
Washington. The NBM which represents the consensus looks 
reasonable with confidence increasing on forecast details. The
NBM may be lagging behind with precipitation amounts. There is 
a disparity between the GEFS (noticeably drier) and the ECMWF 
ensemble and Canadian ensemble (a bit wetter). The moisture tap
wrapping in around the low isn't noteworthy with P-wats only 
increasing up to around 0.5-0.6 inches; however, there is 
favorable dynamics both at low levels and at upper levels. Good 
divergence aloft will feed lower levels with models indicating 
modest frontogenesis over southeast WA and into the southern to
central ID Panhandle. This will create an area of deformation 
where precipitation is favored. Mid levels will also feature 
moderately steep lapse rates at around 7 C/km. The favorable 
dynamics and steepening lapse rates should be enough to 
counteract deficiencies in moisture. I wouln't be surprised if 
the NBM trends higher with its probabilities for measurable 
precipitation and the southeast portion of the forecast area 
will see a good chance of receiving a wetting rain (>0.1 
inches): the NBM currently indicates a 40-70% chance of a 
wetting rain from Deer Park to Lewiston and a 70-90% chance over
the southern to central ID Panhandle (Orofino to Sandpoint). 
Snow levels will be relatively high lowering from around 6,000 
feet to 5,000 feet over this portion of the forecast area. Snow 
levels will be at around 5,000 feet over north-central WA as 
well where light snow is possible over Washington and Sherman 
Pass, but precipitaiton is expected to be lighter and snow that 
does fall may have a hard time accumulating.

We will also have to keep our eye on the convective potential for 
Monday afternoon. Instability parameters are weak with between the 
REFS model guidance only indicating between 80-120 J/kg of surface 
based CAPE over the Camas Prairie for Monday afternoon; however, 
this portion of the forecast area will see strong dynamics Monday 
afternoon. The NBM has a 5% chance for thunderstorms generally 
in the area of the Northeast Blue Mountains, Lewiston-Clarkston 
Valley and the Camas Prairie. Probabilities are higher off of 
the REFS indicating a 15-30% chance over this same area.

Tuesday night through Thursday night: Model ensembles are also 
coming into better agreement with a second upper level low pressure 
system for the middle of next week. There is good agreement on a 
deeper, colder low. Ensembles still indicate some variance in its 
strength though and timing, but overall good agreement considering 
we're still four days out. The low is expected to drop south across 
WA Wednesday into Thursday closer in proximity to the coastline 
than with the low Sunday into Monday. This will result in a 
colder thermal profile with snow levels expected to lower down 
to around 3,000 feet over the Cascades and northern mountains 
by Wednesday night. There is uncertainty with how much moisture 
we will see, but at least light snow accumulations for the 
mountains should be anticipated. This includes the mountain 
passes in the Cascades over to Sherman Pass. Lookout Pass sees a
better potential for at least a dusting Thursday night. Winter 
travel will be possible over this period. Temperatures cool from
being in the 50s early in the week to highs in the mid to upper
40s for most areas by Thursday.
